newsitem.title: USA: U.S. wants to expel Algerian fundamentalist.
newsitem.headline: U.S. wants to expel Algerian fundamentalist.

text.p: United States immigration officials took a senior Algerian Moslem fundamentalist politician into custody after denying him political asylum, the Justice Department and his group said on Wednesday.

They said Anouar Haddam, self-styled leader of the Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) parliamentarians in exile, was taken into custody five days ago and will be detained pending a hearing aimed at excluding him from the United States.
Justice Department officials said Haddam entered the United States in 1993 on a conditional parole request. Once his asylum request was turned down, his authority to remain in the country ended.
The officials said the United States also would seek to deport Haddam's wife and child, who have overstayed their tourist visas. They were not taken into custody.
An American Moslem Council source confirmed Haddam was in jail after having been denied asylum.
An initial, closed-door hearing in the case was scheduled before a U.S. immigration judge for Friday. A hearing on the merits might not begin for several weeks.
France had pressed Washington to silence Haddam since Moslem guerrillas carried out a wave of attacks on French nationals in Algeria and bombings in Paris, diplomatic sources in Paris said.

Haddam was elected to parliament in the first round of an Algerian general election in December 1991 but the army intervened to cancel the runoff in January 1992 and prevent an almost certain FIS victory.

The Islamic party was outlawed and its leaders either locked up or exiled. At least 50,000 people have been killed in the ensuing civil war between the military-dominated authorities and Moslem guerrillas.
Haddam and his family took refuge in the United States, where they lived in Washington and Chicago.

In July 1994, Haddam and another exiled front leader living in Belgium, Ahmed Zaoui, were expelled from the movement's official leadership in exile after endorsing the actions of radical Armed Islamic Group guerrillas, who have targeted foreigners.

He later distanced himself from the guerrillas and represented the FIS at the Rome conference, which established a platform for democracy and peace with the secular Socialist Forces Front and the former ruling National Liberation Front.
The platform collapsed after military President Liamine Zeroual refused to deal with any of its signatories.
Algerian opposition sources said Haddam's influence in the movement was now marginal.
